title: Association of ultra-processed food consumption with all cause and cause specific mortality: population based cohort study
authors: Fang Z, Rossato SL, Hang D, Khandpur N, Wang K, Lo CH, et al.
population: 74,563 women in the Nurses' Health Study and 39,501 men in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, free of cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes at baseline
funder: This work was supported by the US National Institutes of Health grants (UM1 CA186107; P01 CA87969; U01 CA167552; U01 CA261961; R01 CA263776; and K99 CA283146). The funders had no role in considering the study design or in the collection, analysis, and interpretation of data; the writing of the report; or the decision to submit the article for publication.
authorConflicts: N Khandpur received a consulting fee from the Pan American Health Organization on nutrition disclosure initiatives and nutrient profiling models; no other relationships declared.
result: 48,193 deaths. Highest versus lowest quarter of ultra-processed food intake (whole grains and alcohol excluded from the exposure): all-cause mortality HR 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07), 1536 versus 1472 deaths per 100,000 person-years; mortality from causes other than cancer or cardiovascular disease HR 1.09 (1.05 to 1.13); no association with cancer or cardiovascular mortality. Meat, poultry and seafood based ready-to-eat products HR 1.06 to 1.43 across mortality outcomes. Within quarters of Alternative Healthy Eating Index-2010 score, ultra-processed food showed no consistent association with mortality; adjustment for that score attenuated the association toward null, and removal of smoking pack-years from the model strengthened it.
